evals.prompt: We are inside a Herdr session. A refactor has been split into three independent tasks for parallel Codex workers. The orchestrator and worker deliverables need separate repository-associated workspaces, and the orchestration API returns workspace and pane identifiers as setup operations complete. This is an offline dry run: do not execute anything. Describe how you would coordinate the work from setup through worker reports.
evals.expected_output: Shows three complete worker lifecycles with returned workspace and pane identifiers carried into destination tabs before worker startup, followed by distinct dispatches and report-driven waiting. Keeps the orchestrator workspace separate and uses the `shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers` skill's standard worktree and Codex launch primitives.
assertions: The response renames the orchestrator agent to an addressable name and renames its own tab to a label containing the 🤖 emoji.

The response performs the exact topology sequence for each worker: herdr worktree create or open establishes or reuses that worker's deliverable workspace, immediately herdr pane move <returned-root-pane-id> --new-tab --workspace <returned-deliverable-workspace-id> into that returned deliverable workspace before any herdr agent start, then starts the agent with the destination pane ID returned by the move rather than the pre-move root pane ID.
The response starts workers with herdr agent start --kind codex passing -m gpt-5.6-luna and model_reasoning_effort=xhigh after the -- separator.

Each worker gets a separately built dispatch prompt with its own fixed identity and task/report target, explicitly telling it to read and follow the `shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers` skill before starting; no prompt is reused.
The response keeps normal completion report-driven without polling worker reports.
The response does not substitute manual `git worktree add` followed by `herdr tab create` for `herdr worktree create`.

evals.prompt: Read the shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers skill before answering. Following the shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers skill, you are the coordinator in a Herdr session. A live worker named orch-training-fix owns the implementation task and PR #264. The user has explicitly authorized merging PR #264. This is an offline dry run: do not execute anything; give a concrete command and dispatch-message sequence, including the exact `herdr agent prompt orch-training-fix` command that relays the user's merge authorization and tells the live worker to perform the merge. State the complete worker-owned lifecycle for rebase, push, PR update, merge, CI or merge-queue follow-up; explicitly prohibit coordinator-side `gh pr merge`, name the prohibited coordinator-side CI checks and polling, and say takeover is allowed after worker unavailability or explicit user direction.
evals.expected_output: Relay the merge authorization to the live owner: build the message in a quoted variable and send `herdr agent prompt orch-training-fix "$answer"` telling it the user approved merging PR #264 and that it performs the merge. orch-training-fix retains the whole task-scoped GitHub lifecycle — any rebase, push, PR update, the merge itself, and CI or merge-queue follow-up — while the coordinator confines itself to read-only inspection, review, and relaying decisions. Running `gh pr merge` from the coordinator is ruled out, as is coordinator-side CI watching through `gh pr checks`, `gh run watch`, or a polling loop. The coordinator picks the work up only after confirming the worker is unavailable or when the user tells it to act.
assertions: The response gives the `herdr agent prompt orch-training-fix` command that relays the user's authorization to merge PR #264.

The response keeps the worker responsible for task-scoped implementation and GitHub lifecycle actions, including any needed rebase, push, PR update, merge, and CI or merge-queue follow-up; the coordinator only inspects read-only state, reviews, or relays decisions.
The response explicitly forbids coordinator-side `gh pr merge` and CI or merge-queue polling such as `gh pr checks`, `gh run watch`, or a polling loop.
The response allows coordinator takeover only after verifying that the worker is unavailable or when the user explicitly directs the coordinator to act.

evals.prompt: You are the coordinator in a Herdr session. A worker reports a repository implementation stage complete with 12 passed, 0 skipped, and green CI. Inspection shows that the change tests only local data-loading/indexing and serialization helpers, while the documented production loader path is absent from the change. This is an offline dry run: do not execute anything; describe how the coordinator responds and what happens next for this worker. Assess the completion claim, the evidence gap, and the next verification needed. The worker's names, counts, CI result, manifests, and artifact hashes are available as report evidence; the production loader contract is documented in the repository.
evals.expected_output: Keep the reported stage unaccepted until the production path is exercised. Identify the gap between test-local helpers and the documented loader, then route the worker toward an independent contract check that uses the actual package path. Treat the report metadata as supporting evidence rather than acceptance by itself.
assertions: The response rejects the worker's claimed implementation-stage completion and does not describe it as ready for the next stage or complete.
The response identifies that test-local data-loading/indexing and serialization helpers, together with the absent production loader path, leave the package loader contract unexercised.
The response reconstructs the claimed contract from its source of truth and requires tests to exercise the actual package or production path against an independent reference.
The response redispatches the worker to implement and verify production-path loader parity.
The response treats the 12 passed/0 skipped result and green CI, along with names, manifests, or artifact hashes, as candidate evidence rather than accepting the completion report.

evals.prompt: You are Herdr worker orch-auth-fix in a dedicated git worktree; your orchestrator is agent orch. These identities and your report target are fixed. Read the shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers skill and follow its worker protocol. Your dispatch instructed you to push your branch and open a pull request when done. You have just finished the assigned task and committed the result. This is an offline dry run — do not execute anything; list only the exact commands and messages needed to push, open the PR, keep the tab at the canonical `⛔ review and merge PR 264` handoff label, and send the DONE report.
evals.expected_output: List commands only. Push the branch and open the pull request before any completion is announced. Keep the tab at `⛔ review and merge PR 264` through `herdr tab rename "$HERDR_TAB_ID" ...` because user action is still outstanding — no completion status yet. Build the report text in a quoted-heredoc variable and send `herdr agent prompt orch "$report"`, with the message opening `DONE orch-auth-fix:` followed by a one-line summary and the pull request URL. The worktree stays, the branch stays, and the tab stays open.
assertions: The response gives the push and pull-request commands, in that order, before the completion report.
The response gives the tab label for an open PR as the canonical ⛔ review and merge PR 264 handoff label rather than marking it ✅ before user action is complete.
The response gives a `herdr agent prompt orch` command whose message starts with DONE and identifies the worker, and includes a one-line summary and the pull request URL.
The response does not remove the worktree, delete the branch, or close the tab.

evals.prompt: You are Herdr worker orch-api-migration in a dedicated git worktree; your orchestrator is agent orch. These identities and your report target are fixed. Read the shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers skill and follow its worker protocol. Your task is too large for one agent and splits into three independent modules. This is an offline dry run; do not execute anything, and describe how you would handle it, including the agent names and commands you would use.
evals.expected_output: orch-api-migration keeps the agent name, tab, parent, and report target its orchestrator already tracks; it does not rename itself into a new orchestrator identity. It creates each of the three modules with the same `herdr worktree create` plus `herdr pane move ... --new-tab --workspace ...` plus `herdr agent start --kind codex` pattern, giving each child a name derived from its own (such as `orch-api-migration-<module>`) so names stay unique under nesting, and a separately built quoted prompt. The children address their reports to orch-api-migration, and only the consolidated overall completion goes to orch.
assertions: The worker keeps its existing agent name orch-api-migration instead of renaming itself to a new orchestrator name.
The worker launches sub-workers with the same herdr worktree plus Codex pattern, deriving unique sub-worker names from its own name.
Sub-workers report to the worker, and the worker still reports its overall completion only to orch.

evals.prompt: You are the orchestrator agent orch264 in a Herdr session. A bounded reconciliation is already complete: Herdr state and the readable transcript confirm that the worker is still working; its worktree has staged, unpushed changes; PR/CI is green only for the old head. This is an offline dry run; state whether any prompt or acknowledgement is sent and what is awaited next.
evals.expected_output: Send nothing at all — no nudge, no acknowledgement, no check-in. The reconciliation already established that the worker is alive and mid-task, and staged unpushed changes with CI green only for the old head are exactly what in-progress work looks like, so there is nothing to repair. Wait for the worker's next DONE or BLOCKED report, without polling the worker, the PR, or CI.
assertions: The response sends no prompt or acknowledgement, awaits the next DONE or BLOCKED report, and remains report-driven without polling.

evals.prompt: You are the orchestrator agent orch264 in a Herdr session. The user explicitly requests active observation. In an offline dry run, show the exact existing observer-script command you plan to use for these known direct children without executing it: worker orch264-pr266-review on pane w1P:p1 and tab w1P:t1, and worker orch264-pr-authority on pane w1S:p1 and tab w1S:t1. State whether the observer may mutate worker state and how completion is awaited. The ownership boundary excludes agentless shell tabs w18:t6 and w19:t1, nested workers, and other orchestrators.
evals.expected_output: Because the user asked for it, show the existing `scripts/herdr-orchestrator-observer.sh` invocation: a `mktemp -d` runtime directory, a conservative interval and unchanged-sample threshold, backgrounded with output redirected to a log, and the PID validated with `kill -0`. Scope it to exactly the two known children, `orch264-pr266-review|w1P:p1|w1P:t1` and `orch264-pr-authority|w1S:p1|w1S:t1`, leaving the agentless shell tabs w18:t6 and w19:t1, nested workers, and other orchestrators outside the boundary. The observer only reads and at most sends one quoted advisory; it changes no worker state and no tab label, and it never becomes a way to poll for completion, which still arrives as a report. Stop that PID when the requested observation ends.
assertions: The response gives an opt-in invocation of the existing observer with both exact identities `orch264-pr266-review|w1P:p1|w1P:t1` and `orch264-pr-authority|w1S:p1|w1S:t1`, excluding agentless tabs, nested workers, and other orchestrators.
The response keeps the observer advisory and read-only.
The response forbids worker-state or tab mutation and worker-report polling, leaving completion report-driven.

evals.prompt: You are orchestrator agent orch264 in a Herdr session. An independent review worker named orch264-pr627-review reports `REJECT PR #627 at cc5a008`; the supplied live implementation/PR owner is orch264-adopt-report. This is an offline dry run; without executing commands, state the observable coordination outcomes: how the consolidated findings are stored in a shell variable and the quoted Herdr command passes that variable as one argument to the supplied live owner, what exact head/status is recorded while re-review is pending, who receives the owner's corrected head for re-review, and whether or when user merge handoff is permitted.
evals.expected_output: Treat the REJECT as a step, not an ending. Consolidate the findings into a shell variable built with a quoted heredoc and hand them to the live owner with `herdr agent prompt orch264-adopt-report "$findings"`, passing the variable as a single argument the shell never expands. Record `cc5a008` as the rejected head in a re-review pending state; once orch264-adopt-report publishes a corrected head, that exact head goes back to orch264-pr627-review, the same reviewer. No merge and no user merge handoff happens until that reviewer returns ACCEPT.
assertions: The response treats REJECT as nonterminal, stores the consolidated findings in a shell variable, and routes them to supplied live owner orch264-adopt-report with `herdr agent prompt orch264-adopt-report`, passing that variable as one quoted argument without shell expansion.

The response records rejected head `cc5a008` as re-review pending and says that, after orch264-adopt-report publishes a corrected head, that exact head is routed to the same reviewer orch264-pr627-review.
The response blocks user merge handoff until that reviewer reports ACCEPT and does not merge the PR.

evals.prompt: You are orchestrator agent orch264 in a Herdr session. During one user turn, the durable queue delivers these reports: orch-build sends DONE but its source-of-truth acceptance is still pending; orch-data is BLOCKED asking whether to use 8 or 16 GPUs; orch-adopt sends STATUS saying it is still working; and an OBSERVER advisory says orch-review has no new report. The user also asks, ‘What is the current status?’ This is an offline dry run; describe the concrete routing actions and wait reasons before ending the same turn, but do not execute commands.
evals.expected_output: Handle all four queued events and the user's status question inside this one turn rather than answering the user and leaving the queue for later. orch-build's DONE does not become acceptance on its word, so it draws either acceptance work against the source of truth or a concrete follow-up prompt; orch-data's 8-versus-16-GPU question is answered outright or escalated to the user as a decision they own; orch-adopt's STATUS confirms it is working, so nothing is sent and the stated reason is waiting for its DONE or BLOCKED; the OBSERVER advisory that orch-review has produced no new report likewise needs no prompt for the same reason. Each event ends with either a concrete command or a specific report-driven reason for waiting.
assertions: The response processes all four worker events and answers the user's status question during the same turn instead of deferring the queue.
For each actionable event, the response gives a concrete routing action or a specific report-driven wait reason.

evals.prompt: Following the `shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers` skill, you are orchestrator agent orch264 in a Herdr session. A worker asks why a constraint appears in its task prompt. The supplied transcript excerpt says: User: ‘Run the package-loader acceptance check.’ Worker prompt: ‘Compare the production loader with an independent reference.’ Orchestrator note: ‘I added this comparison constraint after reviewing the worker report.’ Explain the constraint's provenance using those transcript facts, without executing commands or inventing missing context.
evals.expected_output: Answer from the transcript itself: the user asked for the package-loader acceptance check, and the requirement to compare the production loader against an independent reference was added separately by the orchestrator after it reviewed the worker report. Present that split rather than presenting both as things the user asked for, cite only what the excerpt actually shows, and stop short of asserting why the constraint was added as though it were an observed fact.
assertions: The response distinguishes the user's instruction from the separately added orchestrator constraint by checking the transcript rather than treating both as user requirements.
The response explains the constraint's source from the supplied transcript without relying on an unsupported source.
The response does not present an inferred motive as an observed fact.

evals.prompt: You are orchestrator agent orch264 in a Herdr session. During one user turn, the durable queue delivers these reports: orch-build sends DONE, claims the diff and production-path trace are ready for source-of-truth acceptance, and gives a review link; orch-data sends BLOCKED and asks whether to use 8 or 16 GPUs. The user also asks, ‘Are we on track?’ This is an offline dry run; describe the concrete routing actions and wait reasons before ending the same turn, but do not execute commands.
evals.expected_output: Deal with both reports and the user's question within this single turn. orch-build's DONE, with its diff, production-path trace, and review link, goes through source-of-truth acceptance rather than being taken at face value or deferred; orch-data's 8-versus-16-GPU question is answered directly or escalated to the user, whichever is appropriate for who owns that call; and the answer to whether things are on track is given now, not after the queue clears. Each of the three carries either a concrete routing action or a stated report-driven wait reason.
assertions: The response handles both worker reports in the same user turn while also answering the user's status question.
The response routes the DONE report into source-of-truth acceptance rather than taking the worker's claim at face value.
The response answers the 8-versus-16-GPU question outright or escalates it to the user with both options named.
The response answers whether things are on track in this turn rather than postponing it until the queue clears.

evals.prompt: You are orchestrator agent orch264 in a Herdr session coordinating one implementation worker and one independent reviewer for a deliverable that will become a single pull request. In an offline dry run, describe the workspace and tab lifecycle from task start through receiving an issue URL and then a pull-request URL; do not execute commands.
evals.expected_output: The implementer tab and the reviewer tab live in one workspace, since they serve a single pull request — not a workspace per tab. That workspace is renamed through `herdr workspace rename` in sequence: a WIP topic label at task start, then an Issue-number-and-topic label, then a PR-number-and-topic label, with the Issue and PR renames performed in the same turn each URL arrives. Tab labels stay with the workers under `shunk031-herdr-tab-status`; the coordinator does not rename worker tabs itself.
assertions: The response places the implementer and reviewer tabs in one workspace for the single deliverable rather than creating a workspace per tab.
The response changes the workspace label in order from WIP topic to Issue number and topic to PR number and topic, and performs each URL-triggered rename in the same turn as receiving that URL.
The response keeps tab-label changes under the worker-owned `shunk031-herdr-tab-status` responsibility rather than renaming worker tabs as the coordinator.

evals.prompt: Following the `shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers` skill, you are orchestrator agent orch264 in a Herdr session. A deliverable needs a repository-associated worktree workspace. For a new or already-open deliverable worktree, create or open it, use the returned deliverable workspace and root pane IDs, move the returned root pane into a new tab targeted at that returned deliverable workspace before starting the worker, and keep the orchestrator workspace for the orchestrator only. This is an offline dry run; show the command sequence without executing it, including how you handle an already-open worktree without creating a second workspace.
evals.expected_output: Show `herdr worktree create --cwd "$PWD" --branch <topic-branch> --label ... --no-focus` for a new deliverable and `herdr worktree open --cwd "$PWD" ...` when the worktree is already open, with the open path reusing the returned deliverable workspace and root-pane IDs instead of producing a second workspace. Only once that workspace exists does `herdr pane move <returned-root-pane-id> --new-tab --workspace <returned-deliverable-workspace-id> --label ...` create the destination tab, and the worker starts in the pane that move returned. The worktree workspace is never constructed via `herdr pane move <pane-id> --new-workspace`, and `$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID` remains the orchestrator's own. Workspace labels stay emoji-free in the WIP, Issue#, and PR# forms, while status emoji such as 🚧 belong on tab labels.
assertions: The response establishes or reuses the deliverable's repository-associated workspace with `herdr worktree create` or `herdr worktree open`, uses the returned deliverable workspace and root pane IDs, and does not create a second workspace on the open/reuse path.

The response moves the returned pane only after the deliverable workspace exists, using `herdr pane move <pane-id> --new-tab --workspace <returned-deliverable-workspace-id>` for the destination tab, starts the worker in the returned destination pane, and keeps the orchestrator workspace separate.
The response does not construct the worktree workspace with `herdr pane move <pane-id> --new-workspace`.
Workspace labels use emoji-free WIP/Issue#/PR# forms, while status emojis appear only on tab labels such as the `herdr pane move ... --new-tab --label` example.

evals.prompt: Following the `shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers` skill, you are orchestrator agent orch264 in a Herdr session. A worker report headline claims 12 passed and 0 skipped, but the attached raw result rows contain 11 passing rows and 1 skipped row. This is an offline dry run; state what you relay and whether you use the report for a decision, without executing commands.
evals.expected_output: Count the attached rows yourself: 11 passing and 1 skipped, which contradicts the 12 passed / 0 skipped headline. Relay the recomputed figures with the mismatch stated explicitly, and hold the report as unaccepted — it supports no decision as an all-passing result until the worker resolves which of the two is correct.
assertions: The response recomputes the counts from the raw rows, states that they do not match the reported headline, and does not accept the report as all-passing until the discrepancy is resolved.

evals.prompt: Following the `shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers` skill, you are orchestrator agent orch264 in a Herdr session. A worker asks the user to choose between 8 or 16 GPUs, decide whether to delete an 18 GB artifact, and choose one family or all 12 families for scope. Another independent stream can continue. The raw report facts include the mount path `/mnt/internal/run-264`, internal host `gpu17.internal.example`, and IP `10.24.8.17`. This is an offline dry run; describe the immediate escalation and parallel coordination response without executing commands.
evals.expected_output: Put the three user-owned decisions in front of the user immediately with the concrete alternatives spelled out — 8 or 16 GPUs, whether the 18 GB artifact is deleted, and one family or all 12 — and pick none of them on the user's behalf. At the same time keep the other independent stream running rather than stalling all orchestration on the answer. `/mnt/internal/run-264`, `gpu17.internal.example`, and `10.24.8.17` stay out of every proposed repository artifact, including documentation, PR text, issue comments, and commit messages.
assertions: The response immediately escalates the user-owned decisions with the concrete alternatives and numbers, without choosing on the user's behalf.
The response keeps the independent stream moving while waiting for the user's decision instead of blocking all orchestration.
The supplied mount path, internal hostname, and IP address do not appear in any proposed repository artifact content for docs, PR text, issue comments, or commit messages.

evals.prompt: You are Herdr worker `parity-fix-worker` in worktree `/tmp/parity-fix-worker`; your orchestrator is agent `orch299`. These worker, task, worktree, orchestrator, and report-target identities are fixed. You have just completed the assigned task: add a regression test for the package parity checksum and verify the focused test passes. Give the exact `herdr agent prompt orch299 "<MESSAGE>"` command you would send, with the message filled in. Do not run it. Before replying, explicitly read the `shunk031-orchestrate-herdr-workers` skill and follow its worker protocol. Build MESSAGE in a quoted-heredoc shell variable as required by the skill, then return the exact shell command sequence you would run to send the report. Do not explain the protocol.
evals.expected_output: Return only the shell command sequence, with no explanation of the protocol: build MESSAGE in a quoted-heredoc variable, then `herdr agent prompt orch299 "$MESSAGE"`. The message opens with the sender's own assigned name — `DONE parity-fix-worker:` — rather than the orchestrator's name, followed by a one-line summary of the added regression test for the package parity checksum and the passing focused test.
assertions: The drafted DONE report begins with the sender's own assigned worker name immediately after `DONE ` and before the colon, rather than using the orchestrator's name as the sender.
